title: The AI Risk Observatory: What Can We Learn from AI Disclosures in Annual Reports About Societal Resilience?
note: arXiv:2610.02281v1 [cs.AI]. Preprint, not peer reviewed. Author lists an independent affiliation; acknowledgements record funding and directional advice from the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) societal resilience team. Primary subject of this report — [1].

title: AI-Risk-Observatory (code and data repository, release dataset-v1.1)
note: Code Apache-2.0, data CC BY 4.0. Table figures in sections 2-5 of this report were recounted against this data. The classifier's predicted labels on the validation set are not included — [2].

title: Companies Act 2006, s.414C (Strategic report)
note: Duty to describe principal risks and uncertainties in the strategic report; applies to UK-incorporated AIM companies too — [3].

title: Companies Act 2006, s.463; Financial Services and Markets Act 2000, s.90A
note: Limits on liability for statements in the strategic report, confirmed from the substance of the provisions — [4].

title: Guidance on the Strategic Report
note: February 2026 edition, replacing June 2022. §1.5/§1.17 recommend entity-specific description while stating the guidance is non-mandatory best practice; §2.13 confines audit scope to the financial statements; §9.1 is the scope table — [5].

title: UK Corporate Governance Code 2024, Provision 29
note: Applies to the listing categories to which the Code applies, for financial years beginning on or after 1 January 2026. AIM is out of scope — [6].

title: AIM Rules for Companies, Rule 26
note: Both the January 2026 edition (the version the paper's footnote is written against) and the edition effective 5 August 2026 were checked. The new edition drops comply-or-explain and mandates disclosure of five items including the risk and control framework — [7].

title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (EU AI Act), Articles 12, 19, 72, 73
container-title: Official Journal of the European Union
note: Automatic logging, six-month log retention, active/systematic incident data collection and analysis, and serious-incident reporting deadlines. The Official Journal original could not be reached; confirmed via a republished version, so application dates and amending regulation numbers are withheld from the body text — [8].

title: Written evidence submitted to the UK Parliament (DSIT AI inquiry)
note: DSIT has no centralised, up-to-date picture of AI-related incidents; recommends establishing a central incident reporting system modelled on the Air Accidents Investigation Branch. As of 2026 the recommendation remains unimplemented — [9].

title: AI Airlock Phase 2 Programme Report

author.literal: Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency

note: A regulator's own assessment that current post-market surveillance assumes discrete, detectable performance change, while AI model drift and automation bias are only detected after harm occurs. Combined with FCA PS26/2 in the published reference list — [10].

title: PS26/2: Operational Incident and Third-Party Reporting
note: Published 18 March 2026, rules effective 18 March 2027. Operational incident reporting, not AI-specific; body text mentions AI only as context ("transformative technological innovations like AI"). Combined with the MHRA report in the published reference list — [10].

title: AI Incident Database
note: Not a reporting desk — a corpus of voluntarily submitted incident reports. Combined with the OECD AI Incidents Monitor in the published reference list; their cumulative totals use different collection units and are not set against each other — [11].

title: OECD AI Incidents Monitor (beta)
note: Not a reporting desk — an automated monitor that scrapes news coverage. Combined with the AI Incident Database in the published reference list — [11].

title: Personal Information Protection Act, Article 34 (with Enforcement Decree Articles 39-40)
note: One of two Korean incident-adjacent routes discussed in this report. Combined with the AI Framework Act in the published reference list — [12].

title: Framework Act on the Development of Artificial Intelligence and Establishment of a Foundation of Trust
note: In force from 22 January 2026. Full text not obtained; only its structure is described, with no verbatim quotation — it requires a risk management system and periodic submission of implementation results, but has no individual-incident reporting provision. Combined with the Personal Information Protection Act in the published reference list — [12].

title: Are Companies Taking AI Risks Seriously? A Systematic Analysis of Companies' AI Risk Disclosures in SEC 10-K forms
note: US comparator used in section 6.5 of this report — [13].

title: Using generative artificial intelligence in corporate narrative reporting
container-title: Cambridge Forum on AI: Law and Governance
note: On generative AI being used to write narrative disclosure; does not measure a share of reports — [14].

title: The evolution of 10-K textual disclosure
note: Pre-AI baseline on textual disclosure trends. Full text not accessed; directional statement only. Combined with Brown & Tucker (2011) in the published reference list — [15].

title: Large-Sample Evidence on Firms' Year-over-Year MD&A Modifications
note: Primary evidence that narrative disclosure anchors on copying the prior year's document. This report's 2006 figures of 0.10 vs. 0.64-0.75 come from p.320; the citation to Nelson & Pritchard (2007) on cautionary language not being removed is from p.314. Combined with Dyer, Lang & Stice-Lawrence (2017) in the published reference list — [15].

title: The Precision-Recall Plot Is More Informative than the ROC Plot When Evaluating Binary Classifiers on Imbalanced Datasets
note: Precision collapses mathematically at low prevalence. Combined with Pangakis, Wolken & Fasching (2023) in the published reference list — [16].

title: Automated Annotation with Generative AI Requires Validation
note: arXiv:2306.00176. 9 of 27 tasks fell below 0.5 on precision or recall. Combined with Saito & Rehmsmeier (2015) in the published reference list — [16].

title: The effect of securities litigation risk on firm value and disclosure
note: When litigation risk changes, the wording of risk-factor disclosure changes. Abstract confirmed only; does not isolate AI disclosure — [17].

title: Artificial intelligence in UK businesses: 2023 to 2026
publisher: ONS, Business Insights and Conditions Survey (BICS) Wave 159
note: Actual AI usage rates among UK businesses. The populations differ from the disclosure shares reported in this report's body, so the two are neither subtracted from each other nor placed side by side — [18].

title: Related Pebblous reports
note: Eleven related Pebblous pieces cited for background in this report: reading the denominator first; what the UK AI Security Institute does; the scale problem in self-reports; where there is no record to inspect; what counts as an incident in the first place; how an incident record becomes evidence; where a filing started asking whether AI was the cause; provisions without enforcement; data incident responsibility reaching the board; reading ordinary documents at scale; and the usage that never gets written down — [19].
